question: What is the file extension of a Java source code file, the kind you type and save yourself?
incorrect: .class
.jar
.javac
feedback: You write source code in a .java file. A .class file holds compiled code rather than source, a .jar is a bundle of compiled files packed together for sharing, and javac is the name of a tool, not a file ending.

question: What does the Java compiler, javac, do with the file you wrote?
correct: Translates it into bytecode and saves that in a .class file
incorrect: Runs it one statement at a time and shows what it prints
Checks the spelling of the text you put inside the quotes
Sends it to the screen so that the output can be read
feedback: javac reads your .java source file and translates it into bytecode, which it saves as a .class file. It does not run anything: running is the job of the java command. And it does not care what your text says inside quotes — only that the Java around it follows the rules.

question: Typing {{1}} Hello.java in a terminal compiles the source into a bytecode file named Hello.{{2}}; typing {{3}} Hello then starts the program.
feedback: javac is the compiler (the c is for compiler): it translates Hello.java into bytecode and saves it as Hello.class. java is the launcher: it starts the Java Virtual Machine and hands it that bytecode. Note that the launcher is given the class name, Hello, with no extension.

question: Match each of these to what it is.

pairs.definition: The compiler: it turns source code into bytecode
The launcher: it runs a program that has been compiled
A file of source code, which a person writes
A file of bytecode, which the compiler makes

feedback: Two tools and two kinds of file. You write Shop.java. javac (the c is for compiler) reads it and produces Shop.class, which holds bytecode. java then runs that bytecode. Write, compile, run — in that order, every time.

question: Arrange the life of a classic Java program from the first step to the last.
items: You type the source code and save it as a .java file
You run the compiler on that file
The compiler writes out a file of bytecode
The launcher starts the JVM, which loads the bytecode
The statements inside main run one after another
feedback: Source comes first, because the compiler needs something to read. The compiler has to finish before there is any bytecode, the JVM (Java Virtual Machine) can only load bytecode that exists, and main cannot begin until the JVM has loaded it. Bytecode is the same on every computer; the JVM is the part that differs from machine to machine.

question: A file holds a program that begins  public class PotionShop {  What does the file have to be called?
incorrect: potionshop.java
PotionShop.class
Main.java
feedback: The file name has to match the class name exactly, and Java is case-sensitive, so potionshop.java does not match. Source files end in .java; a .class file is what the compiler produces. The class does not have to be called Main — it is the method inside it that is called main.

question: NPC: The four parts of every program
intro: Ada unrolls a blueprint with just five lines on it. “Every Java program you will ever read has this same skeleton. Learn to see its four parts and nothing in this hall will look strange.”

steps.say: The first line is the class line. It gives the program its name — here, Shop — and the file has to be saved under exactly that name: Shop.java.

beats.say: The first line is the class line. It gives the program its name — here, Shop — and the file has to be saved under exactly that name: Shop.java.

check.prompt: A program begins  public class PotionCart {  What must its file be called?
check.why: The file takes the class name exactly, capital letters included, and source files end in .java. A .class file is what the compiler makes from it afterwards.

steps.say: The second line is the main line: where the program starts running. Inside it sit the statements — single instructions, each ended by a semicolon.

beats.say: The second line is the main line. You will type it the same way every time. It marks where the program starts running.
Inside main sit the statements: single instructions, each ended by a semicolon. This program has just one, and it prints a line of text.

check.prompt: When this program is run, where does Java begin?
check.answer: At the first statement in main
wrong: At the top line of the file
check.why: Java looks for the method called main and starts with the first statement inside it. The class line only names the program.

steps.say: Every { opens a block and needs a } to close it. Two were opened here — one for the class, one for main — so two are closed.

beats.say: Last, the braces. Every { opens a block and needs a } to close it.
Two were opened here — one for the class and one for main — so there are two closing braces at the end. Count them whenever the compiler complains about the end of your file.

outro: “Class line, main line, statements, closing braces. The next monsters will ask you which is which.”

pairs.definition: Names the program and opens its outer block
Marks where the program starts running
A statement: one instruction to carry out
Closes a block that an earlier { opened

feedback: The class line names the program (and so the file: Shop.java). The main line is the entry point — Java starts with the first statement inside it. A statement is a single instruction and ends with a semicolon. Each closing brace ends a block that an opening brace began, so braces always come in pairs.

prompt: Fill in the three missing pieces of this complete program.
feedback: class comes before the program's name. main is the name Java looks for when it starts the program, all in small letters. And every statement ends with a semicolon — the lines that open a block with { do not take one.

question: Java is case-sensitive: a capital letter and a small one are different. Which of these lines compiles?
incorrect: system.out.println("Hi");
System.Out.println("Hi");
System.out.Println("Hi");
feedback: It has to be typed exactly: System with a capital S, out all in small letters, println all in small letters. Change the case of any one letter and Java no longer recognises the word, and reports that it “cannot find symbol”.

question: What does  System.out.println("Hi")  do that  System.out.print("Hi")  does not?
correct: Ends the line after the text, so later output starts below it
incorrect: Starts a fresh line before the text, so the text sits by itself
Accepts numbers as well as text, where print accepts text alone
Adds a space after the text, so later output is kept separate
feedback: The ln stands for line: println prints the text and then ends the line. The line break comes after the text, not before it, so the first thing a program prints is not pushed down a line. print does everything println does except that: it takes numbers and variables just as happily, and neither of them adds any spaces.

question: What exactly does this print? (Type the output, keeping any line breaks.)
feedback: print leaves the cursor where it is, so Go, lem and ! all land on one line with nothing between them: neither method adds spaces. The first println ends that line after the !, so ok starts on the next one.

question: Two of these lines contain comments. What does the program print?
feedback: Everything from // to the end of that line is a comment, which the compiler ignores. The whole of line 2 is a comment, so the + 10 never happens. On line 3 only the note after the semicolon is a comment, so x = x * 2 still runs, and 4 doubled is printed.

question: NPC: Characters you cannot simply type
intro: Nia holds up a shop receipt printed as one long smear of text. “Everything is on here, and nobody can read it. Three small codes fix that.”

steps.say: Inside the quotes of a String, a backslash starts an escape sequence: a two-character code for something you cannot simply type. \n means “start a new line here”.

beats.say: Inside the quotes of a String, a backslash starts an escape sequence: a two-character code for something you cannot simply type.
\n means “start a new line here”. So this prints Potion, moves down a line, and prints Scroll.

check.prompt: How many lines of output does  System.out.print("a\nb\nc");  produce?
check.why: Each \n ends a line. a is on the first line, b on the second and c on the third.

steps.say: \t is a tab: it jumps ahead to the next column, which lines a list up neatly.

beats.say: \t is a tab. It jumps ahead to the next column, which is how a list gets lined up neatly.

steps.say: A plain quote mark inside a String would end the String early. \" means: this quote mark is part of the text.

beats.say: And a quote mark inside a String? A plain one would end the String early. Put a backslash in front and it becomes part of the text.

beats.code:
System.out.println("The sign says \"Open\"");
// prints: The sign says "Open"

check.prompt: Which code puts a quote mark inside a String?
check.why: A backslash followed by a quote mark means “a real quote mark, here in the text”. Two quote marks together would just be an empty String.

outro: “New line, tab, quote mark. The next monsters want you to read them and to write them.”

question: Each of these String literals is handed to System.out.println. Match each literal to what appears on the screen.

pairs.definition: hi and yo, on two separate lines
hi and yo on one line, with a wide tab gap between
hi and yo on one line, with one quote mark between

feedback: Inside a String literal a backslash starts an escape sequence: a two-character code for something you cannot type directly. \n is a newline and \t is a tab. Because a double quote would normally end the literal, you write \" to get one real quote mark in the text.

question: One of these Strings has an escape sequence in it. What does the program print? (Keep the line breaks.)
feedback: The \n inside the first String starts a new line in the middle of it, so Hi and Yo land on separate lines. println then ends the line as usual, and Ok is printed on a third.

prompt: Fill in the escape sequence each line needs.
question:
System.out.println("Item:{{1}}Potion");    // a tab after Item:
System.out.println("Red{{2}}Blue");       // Red and Blue on separate lines
feedback: An escape sequence is a backslash followed by one letter: \t for a tab, \n for a new line. The slash has to lean backwards — /t and /n are just a slash and a letter, and would be printed as they are.

question: NPC: Type, name, value
intro: Ada lines up empty jars along the workbench, with a pot of labels beside them. “A variable is a labelled jar. Java wants three things settled before it will let you use one.”

steps.say: Read int potions = 12; left to right. int is the type: this jar holds whole numbers. potions is its name. The = puts a value in, and 12 is that value.

beats.say: Read it left to right. int is the type: this jar holds whole numbers. potions is its name. The = puts a value in, and 12 is that value.

check.prompt: In  double price = 4.25;  which word is the type?
check.why: The type always comes first. price is the name of the jar, and 4.25 is the value put into it.

steps.say: The type decides what may go in. Five types cover nearly everything: int, double, String, char and boolean.

beats.say: The type decides what may go in the jar. Five types cover nearly everything you will store.

beats.code:
int cups = 150;            // a whole number
double price = 4.25;       // a number with a decimal point
String name = "Latte";     // text, in double quotes
char size = 'L';           // one character, in single quotes
boolean open = true;       // true or false

check.prompt: Which type suits the number of customers served today?
check.why: Customers are counted in whole numbers, so int. double is for values that need a decimal point, such as prices.

steps.say: You may make the jar first and fill it later. Making it is declaring; the first filling is initializing. Most of the time, do both on one line.

beats.say: You may also make the jar first and fill it later. Making it is called declaring; the first filling is called initializing.

beats.code:
int cups;      // declared: the jar exists, with nothing in it
cups = 150;    // initialized: now it holds a value

beats.say: Most of the time, do both on one line. Java will not let you read a jar that has never been filled.

outro: “Type, name, value. The next monsters hand you values and ask which jar each belongs in.”

question: A named container that stores one value while a program runs, such as  cupsInStock,  is called a ___.
feedback: A variable is a labelled container for a value. It has a type, which says what kind of value it may hold, and a name, which is how the rest of the program refers to it.

question: Write the Java statement that declares an int variable named score and gives it the value 0.
feedback: The type comes first, then the name, then = and the starting value, then a semicolon: int score = 0; Java is case-sensitive, so Int or Score would be different words.

prompt: Fill in the type each variable needs.
feedback: Look at the value. Text in double quotes is a String (with a capital S). A number with a decimal point is a double. A whole number that counts things is an int. And true or false is a boolean.

question: Match each value to the type of variable that holds it.
feedback: A whole number is an int; a number with a decimal point is a double. Double quotes make a String, however long or short the text. Single quotes make a char, which is exactly one character. true and false, with no quotes at all, are the two boolean values.

question: Which of these lines compile?
incorrect: boolean isOpen = 1;
boolean isOpen = "true";
boolean isOpen = True;
feedback: A boolean holds true or false, written in lower case, and nothing else. Java will not treat 1 as true. "true" in double quotes is a String, which is text, not a boolean. And Java is case-sensitive, unlike Python's True: Java takes True for the name of a variable it has never heard of and reports 'cannot find symbol'.

question: Is the shop open? Is the customer a member? The Java type that holds the answer to a yes-or-no question, either true or false, is ___.
feedback: A boolean holds one of exactly two values, true or false, written in small letters with no quotes: boolean isOpen = true; The type name is all in small letters as well.

question: Write the Java statement that declares a String variable named s holding the two-letter text Hi.
feedback: String s = "Hi"; The type is spelled String with a capital S (lower-case string is not a Java type), a single = assigns, and text goes in double quotes. Single quotes are for exactly one character, so 'Hi' will not compile.

question: A cup size is stored as a single letter. Which of these declarations compiles?
incorrect: char size = "L";
char size = 'Large';
char size = L;
feedback: A char holds exactly one character and is written in single quotes. "L" in double quotes is a String, which is a different type even though it is one letter long. 'Large' has too many characters for a char. And L with no quotes at all is read as the name of a variable that does not exist.

question: Which of these would Java accept as the name of a variable?
incorrect: 2cups
coffee-price
class
total cost
feedback: A name may use letters, digits, underscores and dollar signs, and may not begin with a digit. So _price and myVar2 are legal and 2cups is not. In coffee-price the hyphen is the subtraction operator, so Java reads it as coffee minus price. A space ends a name, so total cost is two names. And class is a reserved word: Java keeps it for its own use.

question: A variable will hold the number of cups sold. Which name follows the convention Java programmers use for variables?
incorrect: CupsSold
cups_sold
CUPSSOLD
feedback: All four are legal names, but Java programmers write variables in camelCase: a small letter first, then a capital at the start of each later word. A capital first letter, as in CupsSold, is the convention for the name of a class. Following the convention is what lets another programmer tell at a glance what a name refers to.

correct: The compiler rejects them, since total has not been given a value
incorrect: They print 0, since an int variable starts out holding zero
They print whatever number was left behind in that memory
They compile, and then crash when the println line is reached
feedback: javac checks that every local variable is given a value before it is read, and refuses to compile if it cannot be sure: the message is 'variable total might not have been initialized'. Java will not quietly supply a zero for a local variable, and it will not let you see leftover memory the way C can. Because the compiler stops it, the program never gets far enough to crash.

question: This variable is declared on one line and given values afterwards. What does the program print?
feedback: Line 1 declares cups without a value. Line 2 gives it its first value, 5. Line 3 puts 8 in, and the 5 is gone: a variable holds one value at a time, and the newest one wins. Note that only the first line names the type; after that, cups is used by name alone.

question:
What happens when this line is compiled?
int price = 4.50;
correct: It is refused: an int cannot hold the decimal 4.50
incorrect: It compiles, and price holds 4 with the .50 dropped
It compiles, and price holds 5 after rounding up
It compiles, and price holds 4.50 as it was typed
feedback: An int holds whole numbers only, and Java will not quietly throw the .50 away or round it for you: the compiler stops with “possible lossy conversion from double to int”. The fix is to choose the type that fits the value: double price = 4.50;

question: Match each Java expression to its value.
feedback: + and - are the signs you know. * is multiplication and / is division: Java has no × or ÷ key to use. % is the one new operator: it gives the remainder, what is left over after dividing. 5 goes into 17 three times, using 15, and 2 is left.

question:
A potion costs {{p}} coins and you buy {{q}} of them. What value does this line store in total?
int total = {{p}} * {{q}};
feedback_template: * is Java's multiplication sign. The right-hand side is worked out first — {{p}} * {{q}} is {{expected}} — and then = stores that result in total.

question:
What is the value of this Java expression?
{{a}} + {{b}} * {{c}}
feedback_template: Java follows the order of operations from school arithmetic: multiplication before addition. So {{b}} * {{c}} is worked out first, giving {{product}}, and then {{a}} is added: {{expected}}. Working strictly left to right gives a different, wrong number.

question:
What does this line print?
System.out.println((2 + 3) * 4);
feedback: Parentheses are worked out first, so 2 + 3 becomes 5, and 5 * 4 is 20. Without them, 2 + 3 * 4 would multiply first and give 14. When you want the addition done first, say so with parentheses.

question: NPC: Seventeen coins, five adventurers
intro: Ada tips a pouch of 17 coins onto the workbench. “Five adventurers, seventeen coins. Java shares them out exactly the way a fair paymaster would — and that surprises people.”

steps.say: Java has two operators for sharing things out. Here they are, both working on whole numbers — ints. Deal the coins: everyone gets 3, which uses up 15. When both sides of / are ints, Java does integer division: it keeps the whole number and throws the fraction away.

beats.say: Java has two operators for sharing things out. Here they are, both working on whole numbers — ints.
Deal the coins round the table: everyone gets 3, and that uses up 15 of them.
That is what / does when both sides are ints. It is called integer division: Java keeps the whole number and throws the fraction away.

check.prompt: So what does 17 / 5 give when both numbers are ints?
check.why: Integer division keeps only the whole part. It does not round, either: 3.4 becomes 3, and 3.9 would become 3 as well.

steps.say: Two coins are still lying in the pouch. That is what % gives you: the remainder, whatever is left over once the sharing is done. So left holds 2.

check.prompt: Try one. 14 coins among 4 adventurers: what are 14 / 4 and 14 % 4?
check.why: 4 fits into 14 three whole times, using 12 coins, so / gives 3. The 2 coins left over are what % gives.

steps.say: The pattern: / says how many whole times it fits, % says what is left over. If you want the fraction kept, make one side a double — 17 / 5.0 — and Java gives 3.4.

beats.say: The pattern: with ints, / says how many whole times it fits, and % says what is left over.
And if you do want the fraction? Make either side a double — write 17 / 5.0 — and Java keeps it: 3.4.

outro: “The next monsters will throw fresh numbers at you. Deal the coins in your head.”

question:
Both numbers are ints. What is the value of this Java expression?
{{a}} / {{b}}
feedback_template: With an int on both sides, / is integer division: {{b}} fits into {{a}} exactly {{expected}} whole times, and any fraction left over is thrown away. It is not rounded, so even a fraction of .9 disappears.

question:
Both numbers are ints. What is the value of this Java expression?
{{a}} % {{b}}
feedback_template: % gives the remainder. Take as many whole {{b}}s out of {{a}} as will fit (possibly none at all) and {{expected}} is what is left. When the left number is the smaller one, nothing can be taken out, so the remainder is the left number itself.

question: Which of these jobs is the % operator suited to?
correct: Checking whether a whole number is even or odd
Wrapping a counter back round to 0 when it reaches a limit
Testing whether one whole number divides evenly into another
Pulling the last digit off the end of a whole number
incorrect: Working out what percentage one number is of another
Rounding a decimal number to the nearest whole number
feedback: Every real use of % comes from asking what is left over. n % 2 is 0 for every even number and never 0 for an odd one. count % 12 can never reach 12, so it wraps back to 0. If a % b is 0 then b divides a with nothing left. And n % 10 is the last digit: 137 % 10 is 7. Despite the symbol, % has nothing to do with percentages, which need * and /. It does not round anything either.

question: A price with a decimal point is multiplied by a whole number. What does this program print?
feedback: 2.50 * 2 is 5, and because total is a double Java prints it with a decimal point: 5.0. A double never prints as a bare whole number, and it does not keep the extra zero you typed either — 2.50 would print as 2.5.

question: NPC: Gluing text to a value
intro: Nia taps a line of chalk on the wall: Cups: 12. “Half of what any program prints is a label followed by a value. One operator does the gluing.”

steps.say: Between a String and anything else, + joins the two into one longer piece of text. The quotes hold the label exactly as typed; cups, with no quotes, means the value in the jar.

beats.say: Between a String and anything else, + joins the two into one longer piece of text.
The quotes hold the label exactly as typed. cups, with no quotes, means the value in the jar. So this prints Cups: 12.

check.prompt: What does  System.out.println("cups");  print — with the quotes?
check.why: Inside quotes, Java prints the letters exactly as typed and never looks in the jar.

steps.say: Java adds nothing between the pieces. If you want a space, it has to be inside the quotes.

beats.say: Java adds nothing between the pieces. If you want a space, it has to be inside the quotes.

beats.code:
System.out.println("Cups:" + cups);     // Cups:12
System.out.println("Cups: " + cups);    // Cups: 12

steps.say: You can chain as many pieces as you like, text and values in any order.

beats.say: You can chain as many pieces as you like, text and values in any order.

check.prompt: drink holds "Tea" and cups holds 3. What does  cups + " x " + drink  make?
check.why: The values come out of the jars, and the piece in quotes is copied exactly — including the spaces on either side of the x.

outro: “Label, plus, value. The next monsters mix them. Watch where the spaces are.”

question: Text and values are joined with +. What does this program print?
feedback: Work left to right. cups has no quotes, so its value is used: 2. Then " x " is printed exactly as typed, with a space on each side of the x — without those spaces everything would run together. Then the value of drink.

incorrect: Total: 5
Total:coins
Total:+5
feedback: Java joins the pieces exactly as they are and adds nothing between them. There is no space inside the quotes after the colon, so none appears in the output. coins has no quotes, so its value is used, not its name; and the + is the instruction to join, not something to print.

question: Which statements about Java Strings are true?
correct: String is spelled with a capital S, as it is a class and not a primitive
Joining a String and an int with + gives a result that is a String
incorrect: "A" and 'A' are two ways of writing one and the same value
A String literal may be wrapped in single or in double quotes
Joining two Strings with + puts a single space between them
feedback: String is a class, which is why it has a capital letter like other class names; int, double, boolean and char are the lower-case primitives. Double quotes make a String and single quotes make a char, which is a different type holding exactly one character, so "A" and 'A' are not interchangeable. The + operator joins text exactly as it stands: "a" + "b" is "ab", and if you want a space you put it inside the quotes. When one side of + is a String, the other side is turned into text and the result is a String.

prompt: The int variable cups holds 12. Complete the statement so that it prints  Cups: 12  and then ends the line.
question: System.out.{{1}}("Cups: " {{2}} cups);
feedback: println, not print, is the one that ends the line. The + joins the label to the value, and cups has no quotes so that Java uses what is in the variable. The space after the colon is inside the quotes, where it has to be.

question: NPC: Reading the compiler's complaint
intro: Ada pins up a program with a red mark beside it. “The compiler reads your whole file before any of it runs. When it objects, it tells you where. Most beginners never read what it says. You will.”

steps.say: This will not compile: on line 3 the round bracket after println is never closed. The message gives the file, the line number and what the compiler expected to find there.

beats.say: This will not compile. Look at the end of line 3: the round bracket that opened after println is never closed, and the semicolon is missing too.
The message gives the file, the line number and what the compiler expected to find there. Start at that line.

check.prompt: The message begins  Shop.java:3: error  What does the 3 tell you?
wrong: How many times it has run
check.why: The number after the file name is the line where the compiler got stuck. The mistake is on that line or just before it.

steps.say: Four mistakes cause most first-week errors: a missing semicolon, a missing quote mark, a missing brace, and a capital letter in the wrong place.

beats.say: Four mistakes cause most first-week errors: a missing semicolon, a missing quote mark, a missing brace, and a capital letter in the wrong place.
That last one catches everybody. Java is case-sensitive: System and system are two different words, and it only knows one of them.

check.prompt: Which of these lines would Java refuse?
check.why: System needs its capital S. Inside the quotes you may use any capitals you like — that is just text to print.

steps.say: Nothing has gone wrong when the compiler complains. No program ran and nothing broke. Fix the line it names, compile again, and read the next message if there is one.

beats.say: One more thing. Nothing has gone wrong when the compiler complains. No program ran, and nothing broke.
Fix the line it names, compile again, and read the next message if there is one. Finding and fixing mistakes this way is called debugging, and every programmer does it all day.

outro: “The next monsters are broken on purpose. Find the line, say what is missing.”

question:
This line will not compile. What is missing?
System.out.println("Welcome!")
correct: A semicolon at the very end of the line
incorrect: A capital letter at the start of println
A second pair of quotes around Welcome
A closing brace after the round bracket
feedback: Every statement ends with a semicolon, and the compiler says so: “';' expected”. println is correctly written in small letters, the text already has its opening and closing quote, and braces close blocks, not statements.

question:
The compiler rejects this line. Why?
String coffee name = "Latte";
correct: A variable name cannot have a space in it
incorrect: A String cannot hold a word with capitals
The text should be inside single quotes
The type String needs a small letter s
feedback: A space ends a name, so Java sees two names, coffee and name, where it expected one. Write it as one word in camelCase: coffeeName. The rest of the line is fine: String has its capital S, and text belongs in double quotes whatever letters it contains.

question:
A program contains this line, and isHot appears nowhere before it. Why does the compiler reject it?
isHot = true;
correct: isHot was never declared: it needs a type first
incorrect: true has to be written inside double quotes
A variable name cannot have a capital letter
The word true needs to start with a capital T
feedback: A variable has to be declared, with its type, before it can be given a value: boolean isHot = true; Without that, Java has never heard of isHot and reports “cannot find symbol”. true is written in small letters with no quotes, and capitals inside a name are not only allowed but conventional.

question: Which of these mistakes stop a program from compiling?
correct: Leaving the semicolon off the end of a statement
Leaving out the closing brace at the end of main
Typing system.out.println with a small letter s
incorrect: Leaving a blank line between two of the statements
Indenting a statement with a few spaces too many
Misspelling an ordinary word inside a // comment
feedback: The compiler insists on the punctuation and the exact spelling of Java's own words: semicolons, matching braces, and System with its capital. It ignores everything that is only there for human readers — blank lines, indentation, and whatever a comment says.

question: Arrange these lines into a complete program that prints Hello!
feedback: The class line opens the program, the main line opens the place where it starts running, and the statement goes inside main. Then the two blocks are closed in the reverse order they were opened: first main's brace, then the class's.

question: NPC: Writing a method the tests can see
intro: A wall of chalk, a box to write in, and Nia with her sleeves rolled up. “You can read arithmetic now. Here you write it, and we find out whether it works the only honest way: by running it.”

steps.say: I give you the first line of a method and tell you what it should answer. You write what goes between the braces. The values in its ( ) arrive already filled in.

beats.say: Here is how these rounds go. I give you the first line of a method and tell you what it should answer.
a and b are variables that arrive already holding values. The int before the name says what kind of answer the method hands back. You write what goes between the braces — only that.

steps.say: The tests cannot see what your method prints. They only see what it returns: the word return, then the value.

beats.say: Now the part that catches everyone. The tests cannot see what your method prints. They only see what it returns.

beats.code:
System.out.println(a + b);   // on the screen, and gone

return a + b;                // handed back: the tests see 7

check.prompt: So which line belongs in a method the tests will grade?
check.why: return hands the value back to whoever called the method. Printing only puts it on the screen, and a bare a + b is not a statement Java accepts at all.

steps.say: Press Run and I call your method once for each example, showing what came back beside what should have. Running is free; only Submit counts.

beats.say: When you think it is right, press Run. I call your method once for each example and show you what came back beside what it should have been.

beats.code:
add(1, 2)    wanted 3     you gave 3     ✔
add(5, 5)    wanted 10    you gave 10    ✔
add(-1, 1)   wanted 0     you gave -2    ✖

beats.say: That last row is the useful one: it says which call goes wrong. Running is free and unlimited, so read the row, fix, and run again. Only Submit puts you back in the fight.

steps.say: Java reads your whole method before it runs any of it. If a line does not make sense to it — the compile-time errors you have just met — nothing runs, and you get a message naming the line.

beats.say: One last thing. Java reads your whole method before it runs any of it. A compile-time error anywhere means nothing runs at all.

beats.code:
line 1: A double cannot be stored in the variable half (an int)
        without a cast — Java will not shrink it for you.

beats.say: Read the message before you change anything. It names the line and says what is wrong in plain words.

check.prompt: Your method has a missing semicolon on line 2. How many of the tests will run?
check.why: Java checks the whole method first. Until every line makes sense to it there is nothing to run, so fix the line the message names and run again.

outro: “Every one of these is a single line of arithmetic or text — no ifs, no loops. The whole question is which operator, and in what order.”

question: A potion has a price in coins. Return what a number of them cost altogether.
signature: public int totalCost(int price, int quantity)
hint: One line: the word return, then the price multiplied by the quantity.
feedback: price and quantity arrive already holding values, so the whole body is one line: work out the answer with * and hand it back with return.

question: A gold piece is worth 10 silver pieces. Given a number of gold pieces and a number of silver pieces, return the total value in silver.
signature: public int silverValue(int gold, int silver)
hint: Turn the gold into silver by multiplying, then add the loose silver.
feedback: * is applied before +, so gold * 10 + silver needs no parentheses: the gold is converted first and the loose silver added afterwards.

question: Coins are shared out equally among some adventurers, and whatever cannot be shared stays in the pouch. Return how many coins stay in the pouch.
signature: public int leftover(int coins, int people)
hint: One operator gives what is left over after dividing.
feedback: % gives what is left over after dividing. 17 coins among 5 people is 3 each, using 15, with 2 left — and 17 % 5 is that 2. When the coins share out exactly, nothing is left and the answer is 0.

question: A shop label shows an item and how many are in stock, in the form  potion x3 . Given the item and the count, return the label.
signature: public String label(String item, int count)
hint: Join three pieces with +: the item, a piece of text in quotes, and the count.
feedback: When either side of + is a String, + joins, and the int is turned into text for you. The space before the x has to be inside the quotes: Java adds nothing between the pieces.
